newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China artist unveils handover oil painting.
newsitem.headline: China artist unveils handover oil painting.

text.p: One of China's best known contemporary artists unveiled his own interpretation of Hong Kong's return to China on Thursday in a vast oil canvas crammed with a galaxy of politicians raising champagne glasses. Against a deep gold background, tall buildings symbolising China's march to modernity and Beijing's Forbidden City are framed by exploding fireworks in Liu Yu Yi's work.
"My main concern was how to speak one's heart," Liu told reporters, likening the British colony's handover on July 1 to China's 1949 revolution which brought the communists to power.
Familiar Chinese landmarks blend into Hong Kong's skyline and bustling harbour, with the Bank of China building prominently displayed alongside an array of fluttering international flags.
Liu confessed he had problems deciding who to include in the painting immortalising the handover.

"After long thought, I put in those I knew and understood. My painting has limits, I could just do my very best to have a representative selection," Liu said, laughing off suggestions the list was dictated by Beijing.
No players from Hong Kong's democratic party are pictured, a move which Liu defended as his own interpretation.
Hong Kong's post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa, startlingly realistic, has both hands raised, and is practically brushing elbows with Chinese President Jiang Zemin.
Standing beside Jiang and dressed entirely in black is Deng Xiaoping, China's late patriarch and architect of the "one country, two systems" formula that will govern Hong Kong.
There is symbolism in everything, argued one China-watcher.
"You can always start reading into things, according to who he puts in the painting. Who shakes whose hand, who is sitting next to whom is very important," he said.
Liu said he was anxious to show Hong Kong as an open, international city and so painted in a battery of foreign cameramen pointing long lenses at the clapping, smiling group.
True to the economic fervour gripping China and Hong Kong, the 4.3 metre by two metre (14 feet by 6.5 feet) painting could well be up for sale.
"An object of art can become an object of commerce. If it is auctioned off, I hope it will get a big price," Liu said unabashedly.
Some of Liu's paintings have fetched more than US$1 million.
